title: Suggested Learning Order
description: Google Cloud Platform (Gcp) · Suggested Learning Order. Learn each concept, then apply it in practice.

tasks.title: Linux, networking, Git, Bash (2 to 3 weeks of focused practice)
Docker and Docker Hub: containerize a real app, write multi-stage builds, use Compose
CI/CD: GitHub Actions pipeline that builds, tests, scans, and pushes an image
Terraform: provision real infrastructure instead of clicking
One cloud deeply (AWS has the most jobs; GCP has the cleanest developer experience), then map concepts to the other
Kubernetes: start with kind or minikube, then a managed cluster (EKS or GKE), then Helm and ArgoCD
Observability and security: Prometheus, Grafana, Vault, Trivy
SRE practices: SLOs, incident response, chaos testing

title: Projects to Practice
description: Cloud and Kubernetes features change quickly, so check official docs for current service names, versions, and pricing. description: For system design, the best resource is a mix of Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann, the Google SRE book, and practicing the design problems listed above on paper.

title: How to Actually Get Smarter From These
description: Since the field moves fast, supplement this with recent work from arXiv, the Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind research pages, and annual survey papers. I can also turn this into a 12-month reading schedule or narrow it down to the 30 papers best suited for building AI systems.
phase: How to Actually Get Smarter From These

tasks.title: Don't read all of them linearly. Do the Start Here list first, then pick one field per month.
Use the three-pass method from Keshav's How to Read a Paper: skim (5 min), read without details (1 hr), then deep-read only the ones that matter.
Reimplement the ML papers. Building a tiny transformer, ResNet, or diffusion model from scratch teaches more than reading ten times.
Write a one-page summary of each paper in your own words: the problem, the key idea, why it worked, and what it got wrong.

Read the cross-field papers for transferable mental models, such as emergence, incentives, bounded rationality, and the limits of formal systems. These tend to improve your thinking more than another incremental ML paper.
Follow citations backward. When a paper moves you, read what it cites.

Prompt caching to cut cost and latency
